lessons.title: Selection and Preservation of Farm Timber
lessons.body:
Choosing the right timber starts with knowing your local species. In Africa, good options include mahogany, iroko, teak, and eucalyptus. Avoid softwoods like pine unless treated. Look for straight, knot-free logs. Cut timber during the dry season when sap content is low. Air-dry by stacking with spacers in a shaded, ventilated shed for 6â12 months. Aim for moisture content below 20% before use. Test by knocking two pieces together: a sharp sound means dry.

Preservation protects against termites, borers, and rot. For ground contact, use naturally durable species like iroko or treat with creosote or copper naphthenate. Brush or dip cut ends. For above-ground use, borate treatments work well. Mix 10% borax and 10% boric acid in water, soak timber for 24 hours. For a simple soak pit, dig a trench, line with plastic, and submerge timber for 3â5 days. Wear gloves and goggles.

Charring the surface with a torch creates a protective layer. This traditional method works well for fence posts. Also, keep timber off the ground on stones or concrete blocks. Ensure good drainage around structures. In termite-prone areas, use physical barriers like metal shields or sand barriers. Inspect timber every 6 months for signs of attack: hollow sounds, frass, or soft spots.

For farm buildings, select timber based on use: poles for framing, sawn boards for walls, and durable species for floors. Always buy from a reputable supplier and ask about treatment. If treating yourself, follow safety rules: work outdoors, wear protective gear, and dispose of chemicals properly. Proper selection and preservation save money and keep structures safe for years.

lessons.title: Wood Joints and Framing Methods
lessons.body:
Strong joints hold a timber frame together. The most common farm joints are half-lap, mortise-and-tenon, and notch joints. For a half-lap, cut away half the thickness of each piece where they cross, then bolt or nail together. This is good for corner posts and bracing. A mortise-and-tenon joint: cut a rectangular hole (mortise) in one piece and a matching tongue (tenon) on the other. Glue and pin with a wooden peg or nail. Use for connecting beams to posts.

For quick framing, use butt joints reinforced with metal plates or straps. Always pre-drill holes to avoid splitting. Use galvanized nails or screws; they resist rust. For heavy loads, use bolts with washers. A simple notch joint: cut a V-shaped notch in one piece to fit over another. Secure with a nail. This is fast for temporary structures.

Framing methods: platform framing is common for walls. Build a floor platform, then erect wall panels. Each panel has top and bottom plates, studs at 400â600 mm centers, and a lintel over openings. For a small farm shed, use 50x100 mm timber for studs. Brace walls with diagonal timbers at corners. For roof framing, use rafters and ceiling joists. Rafters spaced 600 mm apart, connected at the ridge with a gusset plate.

Tools you need: saw, hammer, chisel, drill, measuring tape, square, and spirit level. Always check for square by measuring diagonals; they should be equal. Use temporary braces to hold frames plumb while nailing. For strong joints, use glue (wood adhesive) with mechanical fasteners. In Africa, many farmers use local hardwoods; they are strong but hard to nail. Pre-drill to avoid splitting. Remember: a good joint is tight, flush, and reinforced.

lessons.title: Constructing Timber Walls and Partitions
lessons.body:
Timber walls can be load-bearing or non-load-bearing. For a farm building, start with a sole plate (bottom timber) treated and fixed to a concrete foundation with anchor bolts. Space bolts every 1.2 m. Then erect vertical studs at 400 mm centers for load-bearing walls, 600 mm for partitions. Use 50x100 mm timber for studs. Nail studs to the sole plate with two 100 mm galvanized nails. Add a top plate to tie the studs together. For openings (doors, windows), add trimmer studs and a lintel.

For partitions (interior walls), use lighter timber, 50x75 mm. They don't carry roof load, so studs can be spaced 600 mm. If the partition is long, add a mid-rail for stiffness. Cover walls with boards, plywood, or corrugated metal. For a farm store, use plywood on the inside and metal on the outside. Leave a 5 mm gap between boards for expansion. Nail boards with 2.5 mm nails, two per stud.

Bracing is critical. At each corner, install a diagonal brace from the sole plate to the top plate. Use a 50x100 mm timber cut at 45 degrees. Nail with two 100 mm nails at each end. For long walls, add a brace every 3 m. Check for plumb with a spirit level. If a wall is out of plumb, adjust with temporary props before nailing sheathing.

Insulation: in hot climates, use reflective foil or mud plaster for thermal comfort. For animal houses, leave gaps for ventilation. In termite areas, keep wood at least 150 mm above ground. Treat all cut ends with preservative. A simple partition for a poultry house: frame with 50x75 mm timber, cover with wire mesh, and add a wooden door. Always wear gloves and eye protection when cutting and nailing.

lessons.title: Roof Framing with Timber Trusses
lessons.body:
A timber truss is a triangle-shaped frame that supports the roof. It spans wide distances without needing internal posts. For a farm building, a simple king post truss works well. It has a bottom chord (tie beam), two top chords (rafters), and a central king post. Cut all members from 50x100 mm or 50x150 mm timber. The angle of the top chords depends on roof pitch; a 30-degree pitch is common for metal sheets. Use a framing square to mark cuts.

Assemble the truss on the ground. Lay out the bottom chord, then position the rafters to meet at the apex. Fix with plywood gusset plates on both sides, glued and nailed with 8â10 nails per plate. Add the king post from the apex to the center of the bottom chord. For spans over 6 m, add diagonal braces from the king post to the rafters. Space trusses every 1.2 m along the building. Lift them into position and secure to the top plate with metal straps or bolts.

Purlins run horizontally across the trusses to support the roof covering. Use 50x50 mm timber, spaced 600â900 mm apart. Nail purlins to each truss with two 75 mm nails. For metal sheets, use purlins at 900 mm; for tiles, 400 mm. Add a ridge board at the apex. For overhangs, extend rafters 300â500 mm beyond the wall. This protects walls from rain.

Bracing: add diagonal wind braces from the ridge to the wall plate at the gable ends. Use 50x50 mm timber. Check that the roof is square by measuring diagonals. For a simple lean-to roof, use rafters from a ledger board on the wall to a beam on posts. Always treat cut ends with preservative. Use galvanized nails to avoid rust. Work with a helper when lifting trusses. Safety: wear a hard hat and use ladders properly.

lessons.title: Timber Floor Construction
lessons.body:
Timber floors are common in farm buildings for grain storage, animal pens, or workshops. Start with a foundation: concrete strip or piers. For a ground floor, lay a damp-proof membrane (plastic sheet) over compacted gravel, then sleepers (50x100 mm timber) at 400 mm centers, treated against termites. Cover with floorboards or plywood. For an elevated floor, build a framework of beams and joists. Use 50x150 mm beams spaced 1.2 m, supported by posts. Joists (50x100 mm) run across beams at 400 mm centers. Nail joists to beams with two 100 mm nails.

Floorboards: use tongue-and-groove boards or plywood. For heavy loads, use 25 mm thick boards. Leave a 2 mm gap between boards for expansion. Nail with 2.5 mm nails, two per joist. For a farm workshop, use 18 mm plywood screwed down with 40 mm screws every 200 mm. For animal pens, use rough sawn boards with gaps for drainage. Always treat timber with preservative, especially near ground.

If building over a crawl space, ensure ventilation to prevent rot. Leave vents every 2 m. For a grain store, make the floor airtight to keep out moisture and pests. Use plywood with sealed joints. For a simple raised floor for a poultry house, use 50x100 mm joists at 400 mm centers, covered with wire mesh and then boards. This allows droppings to fall through.

Tools: saw, hammer, drill, measuring tape, level, and square. Check that the floor is level by using a spirit level on a straight edge. For a 3 m x 4 m room, you need about 12 joists at 400 mm centers. Always pre-drill near ends to avoid splitting. Use galvanized nails. After installation, sand rough spots. For maintenance, inspect annually for loose boards and replace damaged ones. Keep the floor dry; repair leaks immediately.

lessons.title: Treatment and Maintenance of Timber Structures
lessons.body:
Even treated timber needs regular maintenance. Inspect your structures every 6 months. Look for signs of termites: mud tubes, hollow wood, or flying insects. Check for rot: soft, discolored wood, especially near ground or leaks. Probe with a screwdriver; if it sinks easily, replace the timber. For minor damage, apply a preservative paste or borate solution. For major damage, cut out the rotten section and splice in a new piece, using a half-lap joint and bolts.

Re-treat timber every 3â5 years. For exposed timber, brush on a fresh coat of creosote or copper naphthenate. For indoor timber, use a water-based borate treatment. Clean the surface first, then apply two coats. Pay attention to cut ends and joints. For fence posts, check the ground line; this is where rot starts. You can add a concrete collar around the post to shed water.

Keep water away. Fix leaking roofs, clean gutters, and ensure good drainage around buildings. For animal houses, remove wet bedding regularly. In termite-prone areas, maintain a 150 mm gap between timber and soil. Use metal termite shields on posts. For thatched roofs, replace damaged thatch to prevent water entry. For metal roofs, tighten screws and replace rusty sheets.

Useful tools: screwdriver, chisel, paintbrush, and protective gear. Keep a record of inspections and treatments. Train workers to spot problems early. Simple preventive measuresâlike painting, clearing vegetation, and fixing leaksâextend timber life by 10â15 years. If you see termites, act fast: remove infested wood, treat the area with insecticide, and replace with treated timber. Remember, maintenance is cheaper than rebuilding.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Timber Construction for African Farm Buildings

Timber remains the most accessible structural material for farm buildings across sub-Saharan Africa. It is locally available, relatively cheap, and can be worked with basic hand tools. But poorly selected or untreated timber fails within 3â5 years in tropical conditions, while correctly specified and preserved timber can last 25 years or more. This lesson gives you the practical decision rules that separate a profitable structure from a recurring cost centre.

Treat this as your site reference. The numbers, species, and treatments below are drawn from published forestry and building research relevant to African conditions. Use them to specify, price, and inspect timber before money changes hands.

1. Species Selection: Match the Wood to the Job

In African farm construction, the species you choose determines both the load capacity and the natural durability of the structure. Two properties matter most: strength class and natural durability against termites and decay.

Table 1: Common African timber species for farm construction â durability and typical use
Species Natural durability Termite resistance Typical farm use Notes
Iroko (Milicia excelsa) Very durable High Posts, trusses, door frames Expensive; reserve for ground contact
Mahogany / Khaya (Khaya spp.) Durable Moderateâhigh Roof trusses, flooring Good workability; widely traded
Mvule (Milicia / Chlorophora) Very durable High Ground-contact posts Now restricted in some countries
Pine (Pinus patula / caribaea) Non-durable Low Trusses, purlins, studs (treated) Must be pressure-treated for exposed use
Eucalyptus (E. grandis, E. camaldulensis) Moderate Moderate Poles, rafters, fencing Prone to splitting; pre-bore nails
Gmelina (Gmelina arborea) Non-durable Low Formwork, temporary structures Fast-growing; treat if permanent

Source: Adapted from FAO, Forest Products and Rural Development (FAO Forestry Paper 116); PROTA (Plant Resources of Tropical Africa) wood database; and national forestry research institutes (e.g., KEFRI Kenya, FRIM Malawi).

Business rule: Never put untreated non-durable timber (pine, gmelina) within 300 mm of the ground. If you cannot afford durable species for posts, use treated pine or switch to concrete footings with timber above the damp-proof course.

2. Preservation: The Cheapest Insurance on Your Farm

Preservation treatment typically adds 8â15% to timber cost but extends service life by 3â5 times. That is the single highest-return decision in farm timber construction.

Table 2: Timber preservation methods â cost, effectiveness, and suitability
Method How it works Effectiveness Best for Relative cost
Pressure treatment (CCA / ACQ / creosote) Preservative forced deep into wood cells under vacuum/pressure Very high (15â25 yrs) Ground-contact posts, trusses, poles High (but per-year cost lowest)
Hotâcold open tank Wood soaked in hot then cold preservative bath High (10â20 yrs) Fence posts, small poles Medium
Brushing / spraying Preservative applied to surface only Lowâmoderate (2â5 yrs) Sawn timber, trusses, touch-up Low
Soaking / dipping Short immersion in preservative Moderate (5â10 yrs) Purlins, battens, studs Lowâmedium
Charring + oil (traditional) Surface carbonised, then coated with used engine oil or cashew nut shell liquid Moderate (5â8 yrs) Ground-contact posts (informal) Very low

Source: Adapted from FAO, Preservation of Timber (FAO Forestry Paper 44) and the ITTO/FAO technical series on wood preservation in the tropics.

Business rule: For any timber touching soil or concrete, specify pressure-treated or hotâcold treated material. For roof trusses above the wall plate, brushing or dipping is acceptable if the building is well ventilated. Budget preservation as a line item, not an afterthought.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Timber Preservatives

Creosote, CCA (copperâchromeâarsenate), and many solvent-based preservatives are toxic and carcinogenic. Never burn treated offcuts â the smoke carries arsenic and other toxins. Wear gloves, eye protection, and a respirator when cutting or handling treated timber. Wash hands and tools before eating. Keep children and livestock away from treatment areas. Store preservatives in sealed, labelled containers away from water sources.

3. Wood Joints and Framing Methods

For farm buildings, three joints carry most of the load: the halved joint (for splicing plates and rafters), the mortise-and-tenon (for truss connections and post-to-beam), and the birdsmouth (for rafter-to-wall-plate seating). Nailed joints with metal connectors (truss plates, joist hangers, bolt plates) are acceptable for light farm structures but must be galvanised or stainless in coastal and humid zones.

Rule of thumb for nail spacing in structural framing: 300 mm centres along the grain, 150 mm at ends, and always pre-bore hardwood to avoid splitting. For bolted joints, use 12â16 mm galvanised bolts with washers, and keep bolt holes at least 3 diameters from the timber edge.

4. Walls, Partitions, Floors, and Roofs â Quick Specification

Walls and partitions: Studs at 400â600 mm centres, 50 Ã 100 mm minimum for load-bearing walls. Use diagonal bracing at corners. For livestock sheds, line the lower 1.2 m with durable boards or metal to resist animal impact.

Floors: Ground floors are best as concrete slabs with a damp-proof membrane; timber floors should be raised at least 450 mm above ground with cross-ventilation underneath. Joists at 400 mm centres for domestic loads, 300 mm for grain or equipment storage.

Roof framing: King-post trusses are the standard for 4â8 m spans. Purlins at 600â900 mm centres for corrugated iron sheets. Overhang 600 mm minimum to protect walls from rain. In high-wind coastal areas, tie the truss to the wall plate with galvanised strapping at every rafter.

5. Treatment and Maintenance Schedule

Inspect timber structures every 6 months during the rainy season and annually in dry zones. Look for: termite mud tubes, powder-post beetle frass, soft spots (fungal decay), loose bolts, and split members. Re-coat exposed timber with preservative every 3â5 years. Replace any member showing more than 20% section loss immediately.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Confirm species and natural durability before purchase â reject unmarked or mixed loads.
  • â Verify preservation certificate or treatment method for all ground-contact timber.
  • â Check moisture content: below 20% for interior timber, below 25% for structural framing.
  • â Ensure all metal connectors are galvanised or stainless in humid/coastal zones.
  • â Keep timber at least 300 mm clear of soil; use concrete plinths or DPC.
  • â Pre-bore hardwood before nailing or bolting to prevent splitting.
  • â Provide 600 mm roof overhang and cross-ventilation under raised floors.
  • â Schedule 6-monthly inspections and 3â5 year re-treatment cycles.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • FAO Forestry â Wood and Wood Products â free technical papers on timber preservation and utilisation.
  • FAO â Simple Timber Structures for Rural Use â practical construction guidance for developing countries.
  • PROTA â Plant Resources of Tropical Africa â species-level wood properties and uses.
  • ITTO â International Tropical Timber Organization â free publications on sustainable timber use.
  • KEFRI (Kenya Forestry Research Institute) â regional research on African timber species and treatment.

Bottom line for your farm business: Timber is cheap only if it lasts. Specify the right species, treat it properly, build with ventilation and clearance, and inspect it twice a year. That discipline turns a 4-year liability into a 25-year asset.

quiz.q: Which of these is a naturally durable timber species for farm construction in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Iroko is a dense, naturally durable hardwood resistant to termites and rot.

quiz.q: What is the recommended moisture content for timber before use in construction?
quiz.explanation: Timber should be air-dried to below 20% moisture to prevent shrinkage and warping.

quiz.q: Which chemical is commonly used for soaking timber to protect against insects?
quiz.explanation: A mixture of borax and boric acid is a safe and effective borate treatment for timber.

quiz.q: How long should timber be soaked in a borate solution for effective preservation?
quiz.explanation: Soaking for 24 hours allows the borate solution to penetrate the wood adequately.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of charring the surface of a timber post?
options: A) To make it look nice
B) To create a protective layer against insects and rot
quiz.explanation: Charring creates a carbon layer that resists termites and moisture.

quiz.q: Which joint involves cutting away half the thickness of each piece where they cross?
quiz.explanation: A half-lap joint is formed by overlapping two pieces with half thickness removed from each.

quiz.q: What is the typical spacing for studs in a load-bearing timber wall?
quiz.explanation: Load-bearing walls typically have studs at 400 mm centers for adequate strength.

quiz.q: Which fastener is best for outdoor timber construction to resist rust?
quiz.explanation: Galvanized nails have a zinc coating that protects against rust in outdoor conditions.

quiz.q: What is a gusset plate used for in timber trusses?
options: B) To connect members at joints
C) To anchor the truss to the ground
quiz.explanation: Gusset plates are plywood or metal plates that reinforce joints in trusses.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for roof purlins when using metal sheets?
quiz.explanation: Metal sheets typically require purlins spaced at 900 mm for adequate support.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common timber floor construction method for farm buildings?
quiz.explanation: Timber joists on beams create a raised, durable floor for farm use.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of leaving a gap between floorboards?
quiz.explanation: Gaps allow for expansion and contraction of wood due to moisture changes.

quiz.q: How often should you inspect timber structures for termites and rot?
quiz.explanation: Regular inspections every 6 months help catch problems early.

quiz.q: What is a sign of termite infestation in timber?
quiz.explanation: Termites eat wood from inside, leaving a hollow shell that sounds empty when tapped.

quiz.q: Which treatment is suitable for timber in ground contact?
quiz.explanation: Creosote is an oil-based preservative that protects against moisture and insects in ground contact.

quiz.q: What is the minimum gap recommended between timber and soil to deter termites?
quiz.explanation: A 150 mm gap makes it harder for termites to reach the timber.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to check if a wall is plumb?
quiz.explanation: A spirit level indicates whether a surface is vertical (plumb) or horizontal (level).

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a sole plate in timber wall construction?
options: B) To anchor the wall to the foundation
quiz.explanation: The sole plate is the bottom timber that is fixed to the foundation.

quiz.q: Which joint is best for connecting a beam to a post in a timber frame?
quiz.explanation: Mortise-and-tenon provides a strong, interlocking connection for structural framing.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for trusses in a farm building roof?
quiz.explanation: Trusses are typically spaced at 1.2 m for efficient roof support.

quiz.q: Which of these is a method to protect cut ends of timber?
quiz.explanation: Cut ends are vulnerable; brushing with preservative extends timber life.

quiz.q: What is the advantage of using a king post truss?
options: A) It spans wide distances without internal posts
B) It is easy to build
quiz.explanation: A king post truss can span wide openings while transferring load to the walls.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a non-load-bearing wall?
quiz.explanation: Interior partitions do not support structural loads above them.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a damp-proof membrane under a timber floor?
options: A) To prevent moisture rising from the ground
quiz.explanation: A damp-proof membrane blocks ground moisture from reaching the timber.

quiz.q: Which nails are recommended for fixing floorboards?
quiz.explanation: 2.5 mm (about 10 gauge) nails are suitable for floorboards.

quiz.q: What is the first step in treating an existing timber structure?
quiz.explanation: Cleaning removes dirt and old finishes so the preservative can penetrate.

quiz.q: How often should you re-treat exposed timber with preservative?
quiz.explanation: Re-treatment every 3-5 years maintains protection against insects and weather.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good practice to prevent rot in timber floors?
quiz.explanation: Ventilation keeps the timber dry, reducing the risk of rot.

quiz.q: What is the recommended pitch for a roof with metal sheets?
quiz.explanation: A 30-degree pitch is common and effective for metal roofing.

quiz.q: Which of these is a safety precaution when treating timber?
quiz.explanation: Personal protective equipment prevents skin and eye contact with chemicals.
